sentences: Six men sit together playing their instruments, and in front of them a boy is dancing.
His robes swirl and flap as he moves.
This is A Dancing Boy, known in Korean as Mudong, painted by Kim Hong-do, whose pen name was Danwon, in the late Joseon period.
The painting is one leaf of an album known as the Danwon Genre Album.
It measures 26.8 by 22.7 centimetres, only a little larger than the palm of your hand.
The album holds twenty-five scenes of ordinary people at work and at play, among them the village school, a wrestling match and women doing laundry by a stream.
It is a designated Treasure of Korea and belongs to the National Museum of Korea in Seoul.
Look first at the dancing boy.
His sleeves and the skirts of his robe fly out, and his face is full of delight.
His whole body is moving with the rhythm of the music.
A boy who danced like this was called a mudong, a dancing child.
Boys were usually chosen in their early teens and trained to dance, and the constant problem, records suggest, was that they soon grew up into men.
Now turn to the musicians.
At the upper left, a man in a felt hat beats a large drum hung from a frame, called a jwago.
To his right, a man in a black gat hat plays the janggu, the hourglass drum.
Further right, two men play the piri, a double-reed pipe.
The one in the blue jacket has his cheeks puffed out, putting all his breath into the sound.
Below them come a man playing the daegeum, a long bamboo flute, and a man bowing the haegeum, a two-stringed fiddle.
One drum, one hourglass drum, two pipes, one flute and one fiddle.
This group of six is called samhyeon yukgak.
In late Joseon it livened up birthday feasts and parties and accompanied dancers.
It was, in effect, the most popular band of the day, and you could hire one for a celebration.
Now notice the background.
There is none.
No ground, no house, no tree.
The National Museum of Korea explains that the album mostly leaves out the setting and builds each scene from the poses and movements of the figures alone.
On the empty paper, our eyes go straight to the music and the movement.
Kim Hong-do was born in 1745 and became a court painter trusted by King Jeongjo.
He excelled at landscapes and paintings of Daoist immortals, but today most people remember him first for genre painting like this, scenes of everyday life.
The album was purchased in 1918 and is now kept at the National Museum of Korea.
It first held twenty-seven pictures.
In 1957, the two paintings of immortals at its beginning and end were remounted as hanging scrolls, and the twenty-five genre scenes were bound together again as the album we know.
Step back and take in the whole sheet.
A picture cannot hold sound, yet in those puffed cheeks and flying robes you can almost hear the rhythm of a party more than two hundred years ago.
Today, let yourself move to one favourite piece of music.
